title: Question 6

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain the shape of the line in Fig. 6.3 representing the variation of $V$ with $t$.

markscheme_points.text: p.d. across resistor = p.d. across capacitor; current (in resistor) proportional to p.d. across it; current causes capacitor to lose charge; charge (on capacitor) proportional to p.d. so p.d. decreases
rate of change of p.d. decreases as p.d. decreases

hints: Hint 1: Think about the loop in Fig. 6.1 after the switch is closed. There is no battery, so what must provide the p.d. to drive current through R?
Hint 2: Recall how current in the resistor is linked to its p.d. by Ohm's law, and how that same current changes the charge left on the capacitor plates.
Hint 3: Link charge on the capacitor to its own p.d. with $Q = CV$, and think about why the rate at which $V$ falls gets smaller as $V$ itself gets smaller.
parts.proper_answer: The p.d. $V$ across $R$ equals the p.d. across $C$. Current $I = V/R$ flows and removes charge from the capacitor, so $Q$ and hence $V_C$ fall. As $V$ falls, $I$ falls, so the rate of loss of charge decreases. $V$ therefore shows exponential decay with decreasing gradient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See who drives the current**
You have a charged capacitor connected only to a resistor. Once the switch closes there is a complete loop but no supply. The capacitor itself acts like the supply for a short time. By Kirchhoff's loop rule the p.d. across the resistor must at every instant equal the p.d. across the capacitor, so $V_R = V_C$.

Step 2: **Connect current, charge loss and p.d.**
For the resistor, Ohm's law gives $$I = \frac{V_R}{R}$$ So a large $V$ means a large current. That current is just electrons flowing from the negative plate round to the positive plate, so the capacitor loses charge at rate $$I = -\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$$ More $V$ means more $I$ means faster loss of $Q$.

Step 3: **Explain the curved shape**
For the capacitor $$Q = C V_C$$ so $Q$ is directly proportional to $V$. As charge is lost, $V$ falls. But then $I$ falls too, so the next bit of charge is lost more slowly. That is why the $V$-$t$ graph in Fig. 6.3 starts steep and then flattens. The rate of change of $V$ decreases as $V$ decreases, which is the signature of exponential discharge.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use Fig. 6.2 to show that the time constant of the circuit in Fig. 6.1 is $5.5\text{ s}$.

markscheme_points.text: tangent drawn on Q-t graph and value of Q at exact same time as tangent read from graph
tau = Q / gradient used to correctly calculate a value for tau as 5.5 s

hints: Hint 1: Recall how charge decays with time during discharge: $Q = Q_0 \exp(-t/\tau)$. What fraction of initial charge $Q_0$ remains when $t = \tau$?
Hint 2: Read $Q_0$ from Fig. 6.2 at $t = 0$, compute $Q_0 / e \approx 0.37 Q_0$, and read the corresponding time from the curve.
parts.proper_answer: $Q_0 = 0.90\text{ mC}$. At $t = \tau$, $Q = Q_0 e^{-1} = 0.90 e^{-1} \approx 0.33\text{ mC}$. From Fig. 6.2, $Q = 0.33\text{ mC}$ occurs at $t = 5.5\text{ s}$, so $\tau = 5.5\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the time constant rule**
For discharge $$Q = Q_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right)$$ where $\tau = RC$. When $t = \tau$, $$Q = Q_0 \exp(-1) = \frac{Q_0}{e}$$ That is about $0.37 Q_0$. So if you can find where the graph has fallen to 37% of its start, the time there is $\tau$.

Step 2: **Find the target charge**
From Fig. 6.2 at $t = 0$, $$Q_0 = 0.90\text{ mC}$$ Then $$Q(\tau) = 0.90 \times \exp(-1) \approx 0.90 \times 0.368 \approx 0.33\text{ mC}$$

Step 3: **Read the graph to show the time**
Find $0.33\text{ mC}$ on the $Q$-axis of Fig. 6.2, go across to the curve and down to $t$. You land at $$t \approx 5.5\text{ s}$$ This proves the time constant is $5.5\text{ s}$. Any equivalent method using two points, half-life $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2$, or tangent gradient gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Use Fig. 6.2, Fig. 6.3 and the information in (b) to determine:
hints: Hint 1: Capacitance links the charge stored to the p.d. across the capacitor. Which two graphs give you the starting charge and the starting p.d. at $t = 0$?
Hint 2: Read $Q_0$ from Fig. 6.2 and $V_0$ from Fig. 6.3, convert mC to C, then use $C = Q/V$ and convert F to $\mu\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick the correct instant**
Capacitance is constant, so it is easiest to use $t = 0$ where readings are clearest. At $t = 0$ the capacitor is fully charged and $V_R = V_C$.

Step 2: **Calculate C**
From Fig. 6.2, $Q_0 = 0.90\text{ mC} = 0.90 \times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$. From Fig. 6.3, $V_0 = 7.5\text{ V}$. Then $$C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{0.90 \times 10^{-3}}{7.5} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ Since $1\text{ }\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}$, $$C = 120\text{ }\mu\text{F}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: You now know the time constant $\tau$ from part (b) and the capacitance $C$ from part (c)(i). How are $\tau$, $R$ and $C$ related for a discharge circuit?
Hint 2: Rearrange to $R = \tau / C$, substitute $\tau = 5.5\text{ s}$ and your $C$ in farads, then express the answer in $\text{k}\Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the time constant formula**
For any $RC$ circuit $$\tau = R C$$ You have proved $\tau = 5.5\text{ s}$ and found $C = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$.

Step 2: **Calculate R**
Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$R = \frac{\tau}{C}$$ Then $$R = \frac{5.5}{1.2 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 4.58 \times 10^{4}\text{ }\Omega$$ To 2 s.f., $$R \approx 46\text{ k}\Omega$$
